item.title: 4 Things the Therapy Profession Ignores About Its Own Future
item.description:
Therapeutic Alliance

4 Things the Therapy Profession Ignores About Its Own Future

Why the future of psychotherapy demands a more honest conversation now.

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • If the therapeutic alliance is a primary healing aspect of therapy, some feel it with chatbots.
  • The 50-minute hour isn’t a clinical necessity, and it’s about to be challenged.
  • Competition drives prices down in every market, and ours will not be the exception.

I have spent nearly 30 years as a clinician, and I believe that psychotherapy, at its best, is one of the most powerful forces for human change that exists. Yet the profession is sleepwalking into a transformation it is not prepared for. Therapists are very good at helping our clients face hard truths. It is time we extended that same courage to ourselves. Here are four points that I believe deserve our immediate discussion:

Source: AI-generated with ChatGPT / OpenAI

1. Clients are forming healing alliances with chatbots, and the outcomes data is starting to back them up.

For decades, the therapeutic alliance has been the cornerstone of our professional identity. Not a specific modality or technique, but the relationship itself. The bond between therapist and client is the single strongest predictor of positive therapeutic outcomes across every form of treatment we have studied. It is precisely what we point to when someone asks what human therapists offer that no app ever could.

Except that people are now reporting experiencing that alliance with artificial intelligence (AI). In a 2025 survey of adults with diagnosed mental health conditions who had used an AI chatbot for mental health support, 38 percent rated it as more beneficial than traditional therapy. A 2026 randomized controlled trial (RCT) found that a therapy chatbot produced a 51 percent reduction in depressive symptoms. That same year, a second RCT of nearly 1,000 university students found that an AI platform produced greater reductions in anxiety and greater improvement in life satisfaction than face-to-face group therapy. Furthermore, this is a snapshot of a single moment in time. Large language models (LLMs) mature faster than humans do, and those available today are already superior to the versions used in these studies. What feels like a distant threat today is likely to become an immediate one faster than many anticipate.

My own experience may be relevant here. I have used AI to address some of my own personal challenges. Being a therapist, I came to it knowing how to ask the right questions. Even so, I was not expecting it to help the way it did. I also find myself feeling something unexpected: gratitude. I am accustomed to feeling grateful to the humans who have helped me along the way. Feeling it toward something that is not human is new, strange territory for me.

2. The 50-minute hour was never a clinical necessity.

There is nothing therapeutically sacred about 50 minutes. That structure emerged in the early days of psychoanalysis as a practical way for therapists to see patients sequentially and has persisted in part because insurance companies built reimbursement around it. Clients, meanwhile, are now engaging with AI that is available any time they need it, for as long as they need it, with no gap between sessions where crises can deepen or insights can fade. Of course, the weekly 50-minute hour has value in creating a space for deep work. Nonetheless, this tradition may be modified by insurance companies and chatbots alike. The hybrid therapy models coming to market are largely not built around a 50-minute hour. They offer AI support between sessions, which handles a significant portion of what clients previously needed face time for, and then shorter, more targeted human contact. Less human time, at lower cost, with AI filling the gaps. From an insurer’s perspective, that’s a definite win. From some clients’ perspective, it may be a win as well. But from a therapist’s perspective, it represents a fundamental renegotiation of what the clinical hour is worth, and will likely have downstream impact on the profession as a whole.

3. The profession is not being honest about what we actually ask of our clients.

Think for a moment about what the typical client must navigate just to access care. Finding a therapist who they like, is accepting new patients, takes their insurance, and has an opening that fits their schedule can be a frustrating and lengthy experience. Then comes the endless paperwork—HIPAA forms, therapy contracts, and now the Good Faith Estimate as mandated by the No Surprises Act. Arranging childcare or time off work. And the list goes on. It’s hard to be honest with another human being. Therapists know that clients are always, to some degree, managing how they are perceived. We know not to take clients’ reports of alcohol use at face value, for example, and we are used to clients disclosing critical information months into their treatment. And then there’s cost. Paying hundreds of dollars per session, potentially out of pocket, for a relationship that ends if they move or lose insurance. Being charged for missed appointments, even if they feel their excuse was legit and unavoidable. The impact of a therapist’s yawn. In sum, therapy can be a greater bother than we often acknowledge.

A chatbot eliminates every single one of those barriers. It never has a waitlist. It does not charge for missed appointments. It will adapt its voice, cultural frame, or therapeutic style to whatever the client prefers. It is available anytime, anywhere. None of this makes the chatbot better. But it is a genuinely significant competitive advantage that we are ignoring.

4. Competition drives prices down in every market. Ours will not be the exception.

There is no industry in which the introduction of a cheaper, scalable, always-available competitor has left the incumbent pricing structure intact. Not music. Not travel. Not journalism. Not retail. Plus, the richest companies ever to exist in human history are now pouring resources into AI mental health tools. Insurers are watching the outcomes research carefully. They are already exploring paying for “measurable outcomes” rather than simply reimbursing the hour, and hybrid models that combine minimal human oversight with AI-delivered care are increasingly attractive to them financially. The logical consequence is that therapist salaries, particularly at the entry level, will face downward pressure.

This concerns me deeply. I am not worried about established clinicians with full practices and decades of credibility. I am worried about therapists entering this field right now and those at mid-level who are not specialized. Therapists have taken on graduate school debt, completing low-paid internships, building practices from scratch, all on the assumption that the landscape they were trained for will exist throughout their career. We are not acknowledging that the economics of this profession are probably about to change in ways we cannot fully predict.

That omission is not kindness. It is the professional equivalent of a parent in denial. We have sat with clients whose lives were shaped by what their own parent refused to see about themselves or their worlds. What the parent denies, the child inherits. The newer therapists entering this field are in that position with us right now. They are the children of a profession that is looking away. What we will not reckon with, they will be left to absorb alone. We need to extend to our younger colleagues the same honesty and tenderness we extend to our clients every day.

Of course, no one can see the future, and I am no exception. But discussing these very real possibilities can only empower us as we head into the future. In a follow-up post, I will explore what therapists can actually do. There are real options. But none of them are available to a field that has not yet looked honestly at the problem.

item.title: Rethinking Self-Esteem: From “I Am Great” to “I Am Human”
item.description:
Self-Esteem

Rethinking Self-Esteem: From “I Am Great” to “I Am Human”

Moving from chasing confidence to embracing who we are.

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • Self-esteem asks us to live up to labels. We are not fixed traits, so these labels limit us.
  • Self-acceptance asks us to accept who we are. Self-compassion asks us to be kind to ourselves after mistakes.
  • The goal is not to be exceptional. It is to live our values while embracing our humanity.

For decades, many of us were told that the path to happiness was simple: work on your self-esteem. If you were struggling with confidence, learn to believe in yourself. If you couldn't reach your goals, use affirmations to visualize them into your life.

We kept trying to give ourselves labels like "I am generous," "I am interesting," and "I am beautiful." These permanent identities became impossible goals to live by in every circumstance. When in reality, humans are complicated. We are inconsistent. We can be confident in one situation and uncertain in another. We can be generous one day and impatient the next.

Constantly trying to feel good about yourself actually became the problem. The internal cognitive dissonance struggle of which reality is true settled in. So, year over year, most of us didn't see improvement. In the pursuit of self-esteem, we were either unconvinced, exhausted, or broke.

So researchers began looking elsewhere. And they found that being yourself pays off more socially and emotionally. In non-Western parts of the world, researchers found self-esteem wasn't tied to life satisfaction nor well-being. In many societies, it's other-esteem ("face") that matters. That is, whether you are connected and contributing to others' well-being and happiness helps your own life satisfaction and well-being.

This began to shift our ideas away from the view that we ourselves are a collection of fixed traits that define who we are. And, actually, we adapt when we are a part of a larger context/ecosystem of people, events, and systems. So instead of doing mental gymnastics to justify why in this scenario you are generous and in others you put your own interests first, we benefit from accepting who we are, faults and all.

Moving from self-esteem to self-acceptance

Source: Pavel Danilyuk/Pexels

When self-esteem asks, “How do I feel about myself?”, self-acceptance asks “Can I accept myself as I am, including both my strengths and my struggles?” This difference matters. Instead of trying to live up to labels, we can ask ourselves, "What is influencing this behaviour that seems counter to who I think I am?" Instead of labels, we consider ourselves in a more nuanced manner and develop a self-concept.

A self-concept is simply the story we tell about ourselves. And stories can change. A healthy self-concept allows us to recognize our strengths without needing them to prove our worth. It allows us to acknowledge our struggles without letting them define us. “I made a mistake” is different from “I am a failure.” “I sometimes struggle with confidence” is different from “I am not confident.”

Self-acceptance also creates space for self-compassion. When we understand our own imperfections, we become better able to treat ourselves with the same patience and kindness we offer to our friends and family. When we understand both our good and bad, it helps us acknowledge when we are living our values. And it's in living our own values that can give us self-worth.

Our goal is not to convince ourselves that we are exceptional. Our goal is to aim to live toward our values while recognizing we are human and may make mistakes along the way.

item.title: What Do People Want to Talk About Most?
item.description:
Relationships

What Do People Want to Talk About Most?

Build relationships by indulging our desire for self-disclosure.

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • Individuals find intrinsic value in self-disclosure.
  • People regret missing opportunities to share their thoughts with others.
  • Missing social opportunities can prompt higher willingness to self-disclose to a new partner.

Wherever you live in the world, people are identified and defined by shared humanity. Yet most people have a more intimate point in common as well: They enjoy sharing personal information. Accordingly, people instinctively like you when you express genuine interest in learning about them. When someone is delighted to have met you at a social function, it is likely because they did most of the talking. We are drawn to people who indulge our desire for self-disclosure, and we remember them. Fondly. Research explains.

Source: Image by Rachel Scott from Pixabay

The Value of Self-Disclosure

D.I. Tamir and J.P. Mitchell set out years ago to confirm theories holding that people find intrinsic value in self-disclosure, finding support for this hypothesis through conducting five studies.[i] This value stemmed in part from the independent worth we place in “self-referential thought” as well as simply sharing information with other people. They conclude that our human tendency to share information about personal experience may stem from intrinsic value linked with self-disclosure.

Tamir and Mitchell suggest that people willingly self-disclose to achieve intrinsic value similar to rewards such as sex and food. They found that study participants were willing to sacrifice money to gain self-introspection as a form of reward, especially when they knew their thoughts would be communicated to someone else, suggesting that people view opportunities to share their thoughts with others as particularly rewarding. Tamir and Mitchell also noted that broadcasting personal beliefs and thoughts may generate an adaptive advantage by building social bonds and alliances, eliciting feedback to gain self-knowledge, and making additional discoveries through hearing the wisdom of other people.

Seeking Social Connection

More recently, Seh-Joo Kwon et al. (2026) discovered that people enjoy social opportunities to share information, to the point of regretting missing out.[ii] Recognizing that interpersonal exchange of information is critical to forming social bonds, they note that when some people choose to keep information private, they forfeit the opportunity to make a new connection.

In their research, which studied behavior and brain imaging, they found that participants regretted missed social opportunities, and such missed opportunities often prompted altered decision-making involving switching from withholding to sharing information. People who missed social opportunities were also more likely to disclose information to a partner and be willing to spend more money to disclose to a partner in a follow-up task, which highlights the role of cognitive processes in predicting prolonged interest in the new partner. Kwon et al. note that their findings illustrate the affective, behavioral, and neurobiological processes involved in moments of connection that develop interpersonal closeness and identify activities that bring people closer—such as self-disclosure.

Bonding Within Healthy Boundaries

The value of self-disclosure is best celebrated within the context of healthy relationships. As a career prosecutor, I have seen self-disclosure both used and abused. It is used benevolently within healthy relationships, and malevolently by swindlers and manipulators. So, in balance, self-disclosure should be carefully measured within new relationships until people become more comfortable with their audience, and celebrated within relationships of trust as one of the ways people are wired to become closer.

So, celebrate shared humanity, but share personal information responsibly.

item.title: Fake Vulnerability: 3 Signs Your Empathy Is Being Exploited
item.description:
Relationships

Fake Vulnerability: 3 Signs Your Empathy Is Being Exploited

How to distinguish genuine openness from manipulation in relationships.

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • Fake vulnerability is a component of love bombing.
  • Certain signs can indicate that you are being manipulated by fake vulnerability.
  • Understanding these red flags can help you avoid being hurt by them.

A new partner, who may be a serious problem in the future, can reel you in quickly by agreeing with everything you say. You may think, “Wow, this person really gets me.” However, when they instantly validate your every word without truly reflecting on your viewpoint so they can offer their own unique opinion about the topic, they may be love bombing you. They want to quickly gain your trust, so you invest in the relationship. Once you are committed, this person may abuse the bond to gain control.

During the love bombing phase, your partner may seem like they are opening up. Yet, a person who love bombs usually has difficulty with true vulnerability. They have walls up to protect themselves. Instead, they fake vulnerability by citing past hardships. It may feel as if they are finally opening up, but this may not be the case. Here are three ways to tell if you are being manipulated.

1. Lack of Emotional Depth in Their Trauma Stories

First, they tell you the story of their past traumas, but they rarely talk about the feelings that they experienced during these times. You may easily empathize, and infer how they felt, but their narrative is absent of deep and nuanced feelings.

The difference between real and fake vulnerability: A couple has been dating for several months. During this time, although it is difficult, one partner tells the other about several abusive situations they endured at the hands of an older cousin. They talk in detail about how it impacted their self-esteem and how they were able to recover aspects of their identity once they worked through it in therapy. When the other partner opens up, they state, “When I was 9, my mom left. My dad drank a lot to numb himself… I had to take care of myself. I remember going to school without a lunch or lunch money… I was constantly bullied for everything. It never ended."

Although this list of heartbreaking events evokes a great deal of sympathy in you, what you may not realize is that the narrative is missing a distinct description of the emotions that your partner experienced at these times. Yes, you can easily guess how they felt, but the fact that they do not identify any of their deep and uncomfortable emotions is a red flag.

Without a description of the conflicting and complicated feelings that they must have experienced, they are unable to share how they dealt with these troubling emotions to survive the experiences and recover. When you ask how they made it through, they kind of scoff and give you a general and non-emotional response like, “That’s life. I got dealt a bad hand.” Then they quickly move on to another subject.

2. Inability to Identify Growth or Silver Linings

Second, without an articulation of the deep and difficult feelings that they experienced as they traveled through their hardship, and an explanation of how they grappled with these emotions to cope, they cannot pinpoint a silver lining. Recognizing a silver lining requires you to be on the other side of the hardship, which takes time, and it is an indicator that you struggled with painful feelings, gained insight, and recovered. You can look back and talk about the good that came out of the situation, and what you learned about yourself.

Example of real vulnerability: After disclosing the story of his childhood, Ben says, “Even though my mom left, and my dad drank, my uncle saw what was happening to me. He came over every night after his shift and brought me a snack and tucked me in. He knew my dad was passed out. I always felt so safe when he was around. The shame that I felt at school seemed to melt away when he was with me. To this day, we are close. I also had a teacher who sensed what was going on. She let me stay in her classroom after school so I could paint. It felt like an escape from my reality. Painting probably saved me, and is still my 'go-to' therapy."

If your partner never pinpoints a silver lining, or any kind of profound insight about what the situation taught them about themselves, then they may be faking vulnerability. They want their story to always end badly because they want to exploit your sympathy for their benefit.

3. Manipulation Through Guilt and Shame

Third, you feel guilty about your own life as you listen to your partner list hardship after hardship. They make you feel like their life is much harder than yours. Next, they take advantage of your guilt to get away with selfish acts. They also tend to put you down for your “soft” life.

For example, when they “forget” to meet you and your dad for dinner, instead of apologizing, they lash out, “At least you have a dad. Must be nice. You are daddy’s little girl.” Guilt and shame wash over you because you believe you were insensitive, and you immediately apologize to your partner for having something that they do not.

In this scenario, your partner uses a past difficulty to excuse a wrongdoing in the present. They also make you feel guilty and ashamed for enjoying an aspect of your life by reminding you that they were gipped of this. Their distorted viewpoint is, “If I cannot have it. Then neither can you.” This may be the biggest warning sign yet.

Every human being has experienced trauma, and these experiences can have a grave impact on who you are. However, if you are a person who has worked through past traumas and grown more resilient from them, you don’t need to trump your partner’s trauma with your own. Yet, if your partner constantly needs to one-up your difficulties, it may be a serious problem. Also, if they continually use their past and present adverse experiences as a license to hurt you, they have not done the necessary work of dealing and recovering from their past heartbreak. Instead, they play the victim and demand special treatment. You can find more information on this topic in my book, How to Outsmart a Narcissist, Use Emotional Intelligence to Regain Control at Home, at Work, and in Life.

item.title: The Pre-Parenting Checklist
item.description:
Parenting

The Pre-Parenting Checklist

Research shows the hidden checklist of becoming a parent.

Posted June 29, 2026

Many people assume that having children is primarily a question of desire. Do you want children, or don’t you? But new research suggests the decision is far more psychologically complex. Before people are willing to become parents, many feel they must satisfy an invisible checklist—one that extends well beyond simply wanting a baby.

In a recent study published in Personality and Individual Differences, psychologists Menelaos Apostolou, Alexia Zalaf, and Mads Larsen asked more than 1,000 participants what conditions needed to be in place before they would consider having children. Rather than beginning with researchers’ assumptions, the team first collected open-ended responses, generating 111 distinct conditions. These were later organized into 15 broader themes.

Some of these themes reflected external realities of parenthood: Participants wanted financial security, stable employment, enough income to raise a child, suitable housing, and access to practical support. These are the conditions most often discussed when fertility rates decline.

But the findings suggest that money is only part of the story. Instead, the highest-rated conditions were psychological. Participants consistently prioritized having a supportive and committed relationship, feeling mentally and emotionally prepared for parenthood, and believing they were at the “right” age to become parents. People weren’t simply asking, Can I afford a child? They were asking, Am I ready to become someone’s parent?

This distinction echoes Life History Theory (Stearns, 1992), which proposes that humans allocate limited resources—including time, energy, and emotional investment—in ways that maximize long-term success. From this perspective, delaying parenthood isn’t necessarily a rejection of family life. Instead, it may represent an adaptive attempt to wait until conditions feel sufficiently stable to invest in raising children.

Interestingly, the importance of internal readiness changed across the lifespan. The researchers found that intrinsic conditions—such as emotional preparedness and relationship quality—became increasingly important through young adulthood before declining somewhat later in life. As biological time becomes more limited, some individuals may become more willing to proceed despite not feeling completely “ready.”

Psychologically, this highlights an important paradox. Readiness is often treated as a destination: once we have enough money, enough confidence, or the perfect relationship, we’ll know it’s time. Yet many of these conditions are inherently subjective. Emotional preparedness has no objective threshold. Neither does feeling like a “good enough” future parent.

For many prospective parents, the greatest barrier may not be external circumstances alone but the pursuit of certainty itself.

The researchers argue that understanding these perceived conditions may help explain the decline in fertility across many industrialized societies. As expectations surrounding parenting continue to rise, the checklist itself may become longer, making parenthood feel increasingly out of reach.

item.title: Stop Boosting Your Child's Confidence, It Backfires
item.description:
Parenting

Stop Boosting Your Child's Confidence, It Backfires

Overthinking children don't do well with pep talks but what works is one question.

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • Confidence depends on success but self-trust comes from working past discomfort, and that lowers overthinking.
  • A question like, "Do you want me to listen or would you like suggestions?" goes farther than a pep talk.
  • Self-trust is strengthened by working through uncertainty, not being rescued from discomfort.

Every parent of an anxious, overthinking child does it. Your kid comes home upset. Maybe they failed a quiz at school, got left out at recess, got cut from a team, or got left out of a group Snapchat message about an upcoming party. Your reacting brain kicks in, and you rush in to "help" your child by reassuring them and maybe telling them how to see it differently. The good news is that you are acting like most conscientious parents. The not-so-good news is that, over time, your child is learning that hard feelings are emergencies and require adult intervention.

I see these patterns among the kids I counsel and the parents I coach. Parents do everything right on paper by praising effort, staying calm, and offering solutions. Yet many of these same parents tell me their kids still freeze up and collapse when things go sideways. The missing piece here is not self-confidence, but rather self-trust. Kids who feel confident say to themselves, "I know I can do this." But kids who have self-trust say, "Even if I totally blow this, I won't fall apart." So, for sure, confidence is a great thing when things go your kid's way. But self-trust is what holds them together when things do not go as planned and are disappointing. As parents, we have been so focused on building our children's self-confidence that we've neglected to foster their self-trust.

The Fix Is a Pause and a Question

When your child comes to you hurting, before you cheer, advise, or rescue, try first asking, "Do you want me to listen or would you like some ideas?" That powerful question gives the child the wheel to drive, to trust their inner experience, to decide what they need, and to see you as a resource, not a SWAT team leader.

Consider Ivy, who is eight years old and comes home upset because no one picked her for a game at recess. Her dad wanted to fix it. Yet he just asked first what she wanted from him, and Ivy—yes, eight-year-old Ivy—said she just wanted her dad to listen. She felt heard, which helped her feel more confident about talking to her school counselor the next day.

Miles, 13, was in a bad mood, and his mom picked up on it immediately. Miles reluctantly shared that he had bombed a science test he had studied hard for. His mom used to default to lecture mode, but in this case she just asked whether Miles wanted her to listen or offer suggestions. Miles revealed he wanted to brainstorm, and they did. Miles felt a sense of relief, and felt empowered to talk to the teacher about ways to approach tests more effectively.

James, 17, would freeze each time his family ordered dinner at a restaurant. He had revealed to me in a counseling session that he routinely became anxious about making the wrong choices. I empathized with James's dad, who would feel frustrated and try to speed James up in these situations. I also suggested that his dad approach it from a curiosity angle. So, the next time they were out, and James began to struggle with a menu choice, his dad asked him what selections he had curiosity about. James picked spaghetti, which turned out to be less tasty than he anticipated. But the takeaway for both of them was that they had run an experiment in which James made a choice. His choice was less than ideal, but he learned from it. A few "experiments " later, James began to feel less pressured and more trusting in himself.

The Takeaway

As I discuss in my book, Freeing Your Child From Overthinking, a child's self-trust does not grow from winning. It grows from trying something uncertain, surviving the outcome, and realizing "I'm still okay." So the next time your child is struggling, resist the urge to slip into the first-responder uniform. Instead, ask the question I discussed above, listen for the response—a challenge for all of us parents, and let them lead. The goal is not to protect your children from the inevitable discomforts and disappointments of life, but to help them discover that they can survive them.

item.title: The Dog Beside the Sleeping Bag, a Mark of Capabilities
item.description:
Empathy

The Dog Beside the Sleeping Bag, a Mark of Capabilities

Some homeless have dogs that are loved, well cared for, and physically healthy.

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • When we see homeless people, we only see sleeping bags and unwashed clothes and deem them incapable.
  • Caring for a dog takes planning, consistency, emotional regulation, and responsibility—impressive qualities.
  • We should ask what this person needs to bring their proven abilities to bear elsewhere.

I love dogs. That was the reason that while sitting in a café during a recent trip to London, my gaze kept going back to a homeless man lying in a sleeping bag across the street. You see, on each side of his sleeping bag lay a dog. The homeless man lay there, staring up at the sky, while each of his hands lovingly caressed and rubbed each of the dogs.

Throughout my career, I have worked with unemployed people with disabilities. Many have been chronically unemployed because, during most of their lives, potential employers have focused almost exclusively on their potential limitations. They were asked in interviews what they could not do, and their capacity regarding productivity, commitment, or reliability was questioned. They were mistakenly judged by appearance or a medical situation and ultimately overlooked.

Yet after employment begins, many of these same individuals become exceptionally dedicated and productive employees. They show resilience, loyalty, persistence, and empathy—qualities that were missed in the hiring process because everyone was looking for deficits, not strengths.

After just a few minutes sitting there at the café, looking at the homeless man and his two dogs, I realized that the homeless are another large group of people whom we significantly overlook and underestimate. Many of us instinctively only see the sleeping bag, the unwashed clothes, or the cardboard sign. We judge them by appearance and circumstance and conclude that this person probably lacks the ability, discipline, or reliability to contribute much to society. Most of us deem them incapable, unable, and lost causes.

But move your gaze from the sleeping bag and focus on the dog, and a totally different picture emerges.

Caring for a dog requires planning, consistency, empathy, patience, emotional regulation, and an extraordinary sense of responsibility. These are not trivial qualities. They have many of the same characteristics as employers list when describing an ideal employee.

And indeed, research has consistently found that many people experiencing homelessness who own dogs make remarkable sacrifices for them. They feed the dog before feeding themselves. They walk miles to find water. They sleep lightly because the dog depends on them. Some even refuse shelter, hospital admission, or addiction treatment if it means abandoning their companion.

That should make us pause.

The paradox is striking. Society often labels these individuals as incapable, yet every day they demonstrate abilities that many housed people struggle to sustain.

A person sleeping on the street undoubtedly faces enormous challenges. Some struggle with mental illness, addiction, trauma, or chronic health conditions. Those realities should never be minimized. In the face of such hardships, looking after another living creature every single day while having almost no resources is no small achievement. It demonstrates compassion under pressure, deep commitment, empathy, and the willingness to sacrifice one's own comfort for another's well-being.

Homeless people with pets are not a rarity, as some estimates suggest that perhaps even 25 percent of homeless people look after a pet. And they do well; research shows that “dogs of homeless persons were well cared for and physically healthy”

In psychology, we often speak about seeing the whole person rather than defining someone by a diagnosis or circumstance. Perhaps we should extend that principle to homelessness. Instead of asking, "Why can't this person function?" we might begin by asking, "What abilities are already being demonstrated here? What does this person need to bring those same abilities to bear elsewhere?”

Once we start noticing strengths instead of only weaknesses, new possibilities emerge—for employment, rehabilitation, volunteering, mentoring, and community involvement. Some might even gradually replace their shrouded looks of revulsion with those of compassion or even appreciation as they walk by.

None of this romanticizes homelessness. Having the ability to care for a dog does not automatically mean someone can perform every job or overcome every barrier. But it does remind us that human capability is rarely all-or-nothing.

People are often far more competent than the labels we assign them. Sometimes, all it takes to recognize that competence is to stop looking only at the sleeping bag—and start looking at the dog lying faithfully and contentedly beside it.

item.title: Do Telephone Calls Make You Anxious? You’re Not Alone
item.description:
Fear

Do Telephone Calls Make You Anxious? You’re Not Alone

Are you afraid to pick up a ringing phone or call someone back? Here’s relief.

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • “Telephobia” is fear of talking on the phone, making a call, or listening to voicemail—and it’s not new.
  • Prevalent with Gen Z and millennials, telephobia affects boomers, too.
  • Telephobia is growing, but there are ways to take control.
Source: Dikushin/Getty Images

We’re all busy and have trouble keeping up with calls and voicemails. But a phenomenon called telephobia shifts phone call anxiety to a much higher order of magnitude. We’re familiar with phobias of heights, spiders, crowded rooms, airplanes, and so on, but “fear of phones”? You may have never heard of it, but it’s real, and growing.

While considered relatively new, relegated to millennials and Gen Zers (digital natives who prefer texting to talking), telephobia has actually existed for decades and was first written about in the early ‘90s, years before cellphones or smartphones. One U.K. study found 40% of baby boomers and 70% of millennials reported anxiety when the phone rings. And a 2024 study of more than 300 students revealed 9% experienced moderate to severe telephobia and 33% experienced mild telephobia.

Common Causes and Triggers of Telephobia

Generally, people with telephobia fear what someone else (the person calling or leaving a voicemail; or picking up one’s call) might think of them. They anticipate judgment. Some experience telephobia because of traumatic past phone experience(s), but most with telephobia are simply apprehensive they won’t know what to say, how to ask for what they need, or that they’ll be found wanting in some way. No one likes to be judged, and similar to those who experience stage fright, those with telephobia fear they’ll “mess up,” feel embarrassed, or worse.

Compounding the problem is that almost no one has heard of telephobia, so it remains a quiet, shameful little (or big) secret. This only compounds anxiety and isolation, contributing to people thinking “they’re the only one” with this problem.

At its extreme, telephobia can lead to relationship problems, impaired occupational functioning, social isolation, and more. Imagine if you never answered your phone, reviewed voicemails, or made phone calls for, say, just three months. It could create unlimited personal and professional havoc.

How Telephobia Varies in Severity

While people with mild telephobia feel only a touch of stress upon hearing the phone ring (and can usually answer it anyway), those on the moderate to severe end of the telephobia spectrum can experience total inability to call, answer, or listen (let alone respond) to voicemails. Thus, telephobia presents as a minor nuisance all the way to disabling panic.

Gen Zers, born between 1997 and 2012, are admittedly more at risk, due to less lived experience using the phone (versus online communications). One college in the U.K. has created a class to help students with telephobia, but recovery can be done at home as well.

Tips and Strategies to Overcome Telephobia

Start low, go slow. First, call friends or family you are comfortable talking with face-to-face. Work up gradually to higher-stakes call recipients and professional needs.

Give yourself a break. Let yourself try just a one-minute call to begin, increasing as you become more comfortable.

Use a schedule. Just like “office hours,” agree with yourself to answer phone calls (or make calls, or listen to voicemail) during certain hours, offering yourself time off the rest of the day.

Keep a list in front of you with lines like, “hmmm,” “wow,” or “I need a minute to think about that.” This gives you time to take a breath and relax before responding.

Source: Yan Krukau/Pexels

Ask yourself, what’s the worst that could happen? You hang up and try again later, saying you’re sorry you got cut off (it’s the truth!). Reminding yourself the worst possible outcome is not catastrophic helps create courage to conquer what you fear.

Role-play. Ask a trusted friend or family member to pretend they’re your professor talking to you about your paper, or a boss or customer requesting your assistance. Role-play can help get you ready for any call.

Work off a script. Even a few talking points increase your confidence on the phone. Soon, you’ll likely find yourself not relying on the script much or at all.

Most people with telephobia use these ideas and significantly increase their comfort and ease with phone communication. But if telephobia drastically impacts your personal and/or professional lives, and these tips don’t help, reach out for assistance. Phobia treatments work, and you can recover. Changing your relationship with your phone (calls) can change your life.

item.title: Can Learning a Musical Instrument Later in Life Help Memory?
item.description:
Aging

Can Learning a Musical Instrument Later in Life Help Memory?

New research suggests benefits to learning an instrument later in life.

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • Learning an instrument in later life may help prevent age-related memory decline.
  • Older adults who kept practicing showed better working memory and brain health after four years.
  • Music training in later life offers cognitive, emotional, and even physical health benefits.

It has long been understood that musical training brings many positive effects, cognitively and emotionally. Much of the previous research, however, has focused on children. And in fact, when we tend to think of someone beginning to learn a musical instrument, we often think of kids: a 5-year-old tentatively figuring out a scale on a piano or an 8-year-old squeaking along on a violin as their parents order them to keep practicing. A recent study, however, suggests that the benefits of learning a new instrument may be particularly strong for older adults as well, and may even help ward off memory deterioration.

Back in 2020, researchers at Kyoto University began following a cohort of older adults, with an average age of 73. Those participants were followed for four months while they began musical training with a new instrument, and participants showed improvement in memory performance, along with some physiological differences indicative of this performance increase, specifically in putamen function.

Long-Term Effects of Continued Musical Practice

Over the course of the next few years, participants were followed. While some dropped out voluntarily from the musical training to pursue other hobbies, about half stayed with the routine of practicing their instrument. At the four-year mark, these individuals were brought into the lab and given both cognitive assessments and brain MRIs.

Participants who had dropped out from continuing their instruments showed a reduction in gray matter volume within the putamen, whereas those who had continued with their instruments did not. Moreover, those who had stopped practicing their instruments showed a decline in working memory on the cognitive assessment as well. Finally, there was greater brain activity detected on a broader scale in the cerebellums of those who continued to play, as compared to those who didn't.

Why Music May Be a Powerful Habit for Healthy Aging

It's important to note, of course, that this can still be seen as something of a correlational study, since those who dropped out from playing their instruments did so voluntarily. Perhaps the causation goes the opposite way: is it possible that people who were prone to memory problems were more likely to quit their instrument? It can't be ruled out, though it's important to recognize that in the original part of the study, the gains were seen in individuals compared from before to after the introduction of the instrument. More research could help explicate this.

But all in all, this is another encouraging sign that picking up a new habit—especially a musical one—later in life could have significant benefits. We know that music also can be a mood-booster, a social activity, and a mechanism of emotional regulation—and can even bring some physical exercise. It's hard to think of many other activities that pack the same potential health punch. And the healing power and growth opportunities that music provides may very well stay strong throughout the lifespan.
